headline: A Stem Player Rebuilt from Pure Math, No Polygons Required
lede: A developer claims to have reconstructed a working prototype of Kanye West's cult music device in under 48 hours, using AI-assisted coding and a rendering technique that conjures three-dimensional hardware from mathematics alone. The technical claim is the more interesting one: the device's entire physical form exists inside a single GPU program, with no 3D model files of any kind.

concepts.definition: A mathematical function that takes any point in space and returns that point's shortest distance to the nearest surface — negative if the point is inside the object, positive if outside, zero if exactly on the surface. By combining simple SDF primitives (spheres, cylinders, toruses) with Boolean operations, arbitrarily complex shapes can be built without any polygon mesh or model file.

A rendering algorithm — also called sphere tracing — that works by casting a ray from the camera through each screen pixel and stepping it forward using the distance returned by the scene's signed distance field. Because the SDF guarantees the step size will not overshoot a surface, the ray converges safely until it hits geometry and lighting can be applied. The entire process runs on the GPU with no vertex or geometry data.

A small GPU program, typically written in GLSL or a similar shading language, that runs independently for every pixel on the screen and computes that pixel's final color. In SDF raymarching, the entire 3D scene — geometry, lighting, and camera — is encoded inside a single fragment shader, requiring no supporting 3D assets or model files.

A style of software development coined by AI researcher Andrej Karpathy in February 2025, in which a developer describes what they want in natural language, an AI model generates the code, and the developer iterates by running the output and prompting again — often without reading the underlying code at all. Named Collins English Dictionary's Word of the Year 2025.

@ty_kra_lab's self-coined term for their variant of AI-assisted prototyping, intended to distinguish it from pure vibe coding by emphasizing intentional architectural and system-level thinking. No formal definition exists outside of this post; the phrase resonates with generative art's tradition of artists designing rule-systems rather than individual outputs.

A subculture of competitive computational art, originating in the 1980s, in which programmers create real-time audio-visual demonstrations inside severely constrained file sizes — typically 4KB or 64KB — with no external assets. Demoscene developers pioneered the use of SDF raymarching to produce full 3D scenes without mesh files or textures.

The process of isolating individual components of a mixed audio track — typically vocals, drums, bass, and other instruments — into separate channels called stems, which can then be manipulated independently. Modern separation relies on machine-learning models trained on large music datasets; the original Stem Player performed this separation on-device in real time.

fact_check: The post describes the prototype as “fully working” and says it “lets you mix them directly on the device.” The Stem Player's defining feature is on-device machine-learning audio stem separation — extracting vocals, drums, bass, and samples from any full mix in real time. Nothing in the post demonstrates that this pipeline was rebuilt within the 48-hour sprint. An interactive visual replica that simulates mixing controls without performing live separation would be a significant but considerably more limited achievement than the framing implies. Separately, the role of @wabi requires clarification: Wabi (wabi.ai) is documented as a no-code consumer app platform not publicly associated with GLSL shader programming, raising an open question about whether @wabi refers to this platform or to a different individual collaborator.
